title: The baby blues, and how to tell when it's more than that
author: Shayla Martinez-O'Brien, LPC
excerpt: Baby blues, postpartum depression and postpartum anxiety get talked about as one thing. They aren't, and knowing which one you're in changes what actually helps.
heroAlt: Ashley LeRossignol and Shayla Martinez-O'Brien, co-facilitators of Mama's Golden Hour, standing together outdoors beneath a cottonwood.
body: Almost every new mother cries more easily than usual in the first couple of weeks after birth. Almost every new mother is told this is normal. Both of those things are true, which is part of what makes it so hard to tell, later, whether what you're feeling is still that — or something that needs more than time.

The baby blues shows up in the first few days after birth, driven largely by the sharp hormonal drop that follows delivery, plus exhaustion and the sheer shock of it. It looks like tearfulness, mood swings, irritability, trouble sleeping even when the baby is asleep. It's uncomfortable, and it's common enough to be considered part of a typical postpartum course. The defining feature is that it lifts on its own, usually within two weeks, without treatment.

Postpartum depression is a different thing wearing similar clothes. It can start any time in the first year, not just the first weeks, and it doesn't resolve by itself the way the baby blues does. It tends to include a persistent low mood or numbness, losing interest in things that used to matter, guilt that feels disproportionate to anything you've actually done, and sometimes a frightening sense of disconnection from the baby. If two weeks have passed and it hasn't lifted — or it's gotten heavier instead of lighter — that's the signal to take it further than waiting it out.
## Anxiety doesn't always look like sadness

A lot of postpartum struggle gets missed because people are watching for sadness and what's actually there is anxiety. Postpartum anxiety can mean a racing, looping mind, a constant sense that something is about to go wrong, checking on the baby's breathing over and over, or intrusive thoughts that arrive uninvited and feel completely out of character. Those thoughts are common and they are not a sign that something is wrong with you as a mother — but they're also not something to sit with alone if they're frequent or distressing.

The concrete, unglamorous truth is that support helps — the kind that doesn't require you to have it together first. That can be individual therapy, it can be a group of other mothers who don't need the situation explained to them, and it's very often both. Medication is sometimes part of it too, and that's a conversation for a doctor rather than a blog post, but it's worth knowing it's on the table and it doesn't mean you failed at something.

If any of this sounds familiar, you don't need a diagnosis in hand before reaching out — a first conversation is free and fifteen minutes, and part of its purpose is simply figuring out what kind of support actually fits. Mama's Golden Hour is a six-week group for exactly this stretch of motherhood, alongside individual therapy for anyone who wants that instead or as well.
